analysis.investment_thesis: MedPlus is a competent pharmacy retailer riding India's organized pharma tailwind, but its 8.8% ROE, 4.75% operating margins, and zero R&D make it antithetical to Fisher's vision of an exceptional growth company with an innovation moat. At 50x earnings for a thin-margin distributor with 15% revenue CAGR, the market is pricing in far more durability than the business model warrants.
key_strengths: India organized pharma retail TAM is large with ~10-15% penetration, offering a long runway for store-count growth
Operating leverage is real — EBITDA CAGR (30.9%) materially outpaces revenue CAGR (15.1%) over 9 years
FY25 free cash flow surged to INR 482 Cr, signaling the store base is maturing and capex intensity is falling
key_risks: ROE of 8.8% and ROCE of 10.3% are structurally weak — far below Fisher's 20%+ threshold and barely above cost of capital
Borrowings have risen every single year (INR 477 Cr → 1,193 Cr), creating fragility in a low-margin, high-lease-liability retail model
No R&D, no proprietary product pipeline — this is pure execution/distribution with no innovation moat; easily replicable by Reliance, PharmEasy, or Apollo Pharmacy
red_flags: Net profit nearly wiped out in FY2019 (INR 12 Cr) and FY2020 (INR 2 Cr) — extreme earnings fragility in downturns
Operating margin of 4.75% leaves almost no room for error on rising rent, labor, or competitive pricing pressure
P/E of 50.9x on a business with sub-10% ROE is a dangerous valuation gap
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my scuttlebutt perspective, the pharmacy retail sector in India has genuine secular tailwinds — chronic disease burden, rising insurance penetration, shift from unorganized kiranas to organized chains. MedPlus has executed reasonably, scaling revenue from INR 1,733 Cr to INR 6,136 Cr over nine years. But 15.1% revenue CAGR, while respectable, falls short of the 20-30% I demand. More troubling is what the business *is*: a distributor of other people's branded medicines, competing on location density and price. Private labels and diagnostics are nascent positives, but they contribute marginally to a 4.75% operating margin that offers no buffer against competition from deep-pocketed rivals like Reliance Retail or Apollo Pharmacy.

The financial profile fails nearly every Fisher quality screen. ROE of 8.8% — after nine years of scale-building — tells me this business does not earn exceptional returns on incremental capital. Debt has compounded at 22% annually even as the company raised equity via its 2021 IPO. The FY25 FCF surge to INR 482 Cr is encouraging and suggests store-level maturity, but I need to see sustained high-ROE compounding, not a single year's cash harvest. At 50x earnings and EV/EBITDA of 28x, the market is pricing MedPlus like an innovation-driven compounder — it is not one. I would only revisit at a meaningful valuation discount with evidence that private-label margins are structurally lifting ROE above 15%.
